posts.body:
4,248 leads. One test most people never run.

Cheap leads and leads that close are two different products. You only find out which one you built if you test the gap between the click and the phone call.

Here is the test. Open your own ad, the one running right now. Fill in the lead form yourself, with your own number. Start a timer the second you hit submit.

Then wait. Not for a callback window someone promised you. For the actual ring.

At Nova Attire, a Tirupur apparel manufacturer, 4,248 wholesale buyer leads came in at ₹16.58 each across six campaigns. They tracked every one live in a Google Sheet. Only about 5-6% were junk. The rest were right for their niche, and sample orders followed, then one or two bulk orders each.

What never got built was what happens after. No reorder timing. No follow-up for when a buyer's stock would run low. A lead who said "not interested" was closed for good — and some of those came back and ordered anyway, on their own.

The leads were never the problem. The second order was.

Run the test on your own form this week. How many minutes passed between your submit and your phone ringing?

posts.body:
4,248 leads at ₹16.58 each.

That is a real number. Nova Attire, a Tirupur apparel manufacturer, spent ₹70,444 across six campaigns and Meta's Ads Manager counted every one of those leads against the ad and form that produced it.

Cheap leads and leads that close are two different products.

The form asked nothing hard. Fill a lead form on Facebook or Instagram, and it pre-fills your name, phone and email from your profile. Two taps and you are done. So Meta went looking for the cheapest person who would do a thing that cost them nothing to do — which is exactly what the form asked for.

Nova Attire tracked every lead live in a sheet and said only about 5-6% were junk. The rest were relevant to their niche. Leads turned into sample orders and one or two bulk orders each. But nothing was built to catch the second order — no reminder when a buyer's stock would run low, no follow-up on "maybe later." A few of those buyers came back on their own anyway.

Nobody ever recorded how many of the 4,248 became repeat orders. Including me.

That is the number I would build a system to catch first, before I ever chased a cheaper cost per lead again.

What does your own cost-per-lead number actually tell you about repeat business?

posts.hook: 4,248 leads at ₹16.58 each. Cheap leads and leads that close are two different products.
posts.body:
4,248 leads at ₹16.58 each.

Cheap leads and leads that close are two different products.

That number came from a Tirupur apparel manufacturer, across six campaigns, spending ₹70,444 in total. The ad asked for the least effort possible. So Meta went looking for the cheapest person who would submit a form — which is exactly what it was asked to find.

Nobody ever recorded how many of those 4,248 became orders. Including me. Nothing ever sent that outcome back to Meta, so it kept optimising for form fills, not for buyers.

Compare that to a different campaign, for a UK wholesale apparel brand. The ad and form stated a 200-piece minimum order upfront. It brought in 19 responses, at under $6 an enquiry each. Far fewer people, but every one of them had read the one line that scares off anyone not actually placing a bulk order.

That is the whole method. Before you launch a lead form, add the one line that describes the real cost of being your customer — a minimum order, a price range, a commitment. It will not make your cost per lead look good on a report. It will make the leads underneath it worth something.

I put a free checklist for writing that line on my site, if you want to run it against your own form this week.

What does your lead form currently ask a stranger to do?
